summary: Describes techniques that let LISP sites communicate with Internet sites not running LISP, using IPv4, IPv6 or both. LISP sites use endpoint identifiers instead of ordinary addresses, so special helper devices are needed. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) sites use endpoint identifiers that ordinary Internet routes may not carry. This RFC describes three ways to let those sites exchange packets with sites that do not use LISP.

questions: how do lisp sites talk to non-lisp sites
how do lisp sites reach non-lisp sites
subtitle: Three ways for LISP and ordinary IP sites to exchange traffic.

tldr.problem: LISP sites use endpoint identifiers that are normally absent from Internet routing, so sites without LISP may not be able to reach them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes Proxy-ITRs, Proxy-ETRs and LISP-NAT. Each provides a different way to route, encapsulate or translate packets between LISP and non-LISP sites.
tldr.outcome: The mechanisms are experimental. The RFC says deployment effects and impacts on applications still need study.

today: RFC 6832 is an Experimental specification published in January 2013, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says that effects on traffic and applications still need further study.

sections.title: Why LISP Needs Interworking
sections.content:
The Locator/ID Separation Protocol (LISP) uses endpoint identifiers (EIDs) for the source and destination of traffic. The global routing system normally carries routes to routing locators (RLOCs), not to EID prefixes, so a non-LISP site may have no route to a LISP site's EID.

RFC 6832 describes three ways to bridge that gap: a Proxy Ingress Tunnel Router (Proxy-ITR), a Proxy Egress Tunnel Router (Proxy-ETR), and LISP Network Address Translation (LISP-NAT). The choice depends on which direction packets need help and whether address translation is suitable.
sections.plainLanguage: A LISP endpoint identifier can name a destination without giving ordinary Internet routers a route to it. The RFC describes helpers that provide the missing path or replace the address.

sections.title: The Four Traffic Directions
sections.content:
The RFC separates four cases: non-LISP to non-LISP, LISP to LISP, LISP to non-LISP, and non-LISP to LISP. The first uses ordinary Internet routing, while LISP-to-LISP communication is described by RFC 6830.

A LISP site can usually send to a non-LISP destination without encapsulation because that destination has a routable prefix. The harder direction is a non-LISP host sending to a non-routable EID; without an interworking mechanism, a router with no route can drop the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: Traffic between two LISP sites and traffic between two ordinary sites already have their own routing paths. The difficult case is an ordinary site sending to a LISP identifier that has no public route.

sections.title: Proxy Routers and Address Translation
sections.content:
A Proxy-ITR advertises aggregated EID prefixes into parts of the public routing system. It receives traffic from non-LISP sites, looks up the destination mapping, and encapsulates the packet toward a LISP site's RLOC. The reply can travel natively and skip the Proxy-ITR.

A Proxy-ETR receives LISP-encapsulated traffic for non-LISP destinations, removes the outer LISP header, and forwards the original packet. LISP-NAT instead replaces a non-routable source EID with a routable address and keeps a mapping so replies can be translated back to the host.
sections.plainLanguage: A Proxy-ITR wraps traffic headed into LISP and sends it toward the destination locator. A Proxy-ETR removes that wrapper on traffic leaving LISP, while LISP-NAT changes addresses and records how to reverse the change.

sections.title: Costs, Placement and Security
sections.content:
Proxy-ITRs should be close to non-LISP sites so their route announcements stay limited and their traffic load can be shared. Proxy-ETRs are best placed near the LISP sites they serve. These helpers may be run by another organization, so the RFC advises checking that provider's service quality.

A Proxy-ETR should check the inner source EID against configured LISP sites to prevent spoofed sources. Proxy devices can inspect traffic, and LISP-NAT hides a host's non-routable EID behind a routable address. The RFC says several effects on applications and Internet traffic require further analysis.
sections.plainLanguage: Where a proxy sits changes the route packets take, and a proxy operator can inspect traffic passing through it. A Proxy-ETR should check that an inner source address belongs to a configured LISP site.
